name: Tan lines meta

lead: Tan lines are the contrast between skin exposed to sun and skin covered by clothing or swimwear. Some people try to avoid them with tan-through clothing or sun exposure of covered areas, while others keep them for effect.
No clinical studies on tan line management as an appearance strategy were found.

paras: Tanning occurs when melanocytes make melanin in response to UV; covered skin does not receive UV, so it stays lighter.[1] People managing tan lines adjust clothing, positioning or use sunless tanners to even out colour.[2]

Added UV exposure to even a tan raises the risk of sunburn, premature aging and skin cancer.[1] Sunless products avoid UV but can streak or look orange if applied unevenly, and bronzers can rub off on clothing.[2]

lead: Tan lines are visible boundaries between tanned skin and skin that was covered, for example by swimwear or a watch strap. In appearance-focused communities, the term 'tan lines meta' refers to deliberately managing them, either to avoid them for an even tan or to display them.

Tan-through swimwear was introduced in 1969, and a Coppertone advertisement from 1953 famously depicted a child's tan line, according to Wikipedia.[1] Sunless tanning products are another route to evening out colour without added UV exposure.[2]

paras: A tan line forms because melanin production is triggered by UV exposure and covered skin gets less of it.[1] Managing tan lines can mean wearing minimal or tan-through clothing, repositioning during sun exposure, or blending the boundary with a sunless tanner or bronzer.[1][2]
Before the 1920s, a tan was associated with outdoor labour, and its fashionability grew afterwards; tan-through swimwear appeared in 1969 and tanning beds in 1978.[1]

Frequent UV exposure is associated with sunburn, skin aging and skin cancer, and a 2010 study cited by Wikipedia linked frequent tanning bed use to about triple the melanoma risk.[1] DHA self-tanners are reported to produce orange or splotchy results when misapplied.[2]
